cards.title: Zdania wstawiane w lukę: jak dobierać
cards.tip: Przekreślaj wykorzystane fragmenty. Na końcu sprawdź, czy tekst czyta się płynnie.

cards.title: Teksty popularnonaukowe: stopnie pewności
cards.body:
Autorzy artykułów rzadko piszą kategorycznie. **Hedging** – słowa łagodzące – zmienia prawdziwość zdania:
**suggest, may, might, seem, appear, often, some, tend to** – możliwość, nie pewność;
**prove, show, always, never, all, definitely** – pewność.
Zdanie typu "studies suggest that A" nie potwierdza, że A jest udowodnione.

cards.title: TRUE/FALSE na poziomie rejonowym
cards.body:
Zdania są często **uogólnieniem lub zmianą szczegółu**: tekst mówi o niektórych, a zdanie o wszystkich; tekst o jednej osobie, a zdanie o grupie; tekst o planie, a zdanie o decyzji.
Sprawdź także **przyczynę i skutek** (because, led to, as a result) oraz **autora** wypowiedzi: czy opinia należy do krytyków, do badaczy czy do autora tekstu.

cards.title: Czas w arkuszu rejonowym
cards.body:
Arkusz rejonowy trwa **90 minut** i ma **100 punktów**.
Długie zadania z tekstem (czytanie, luki, brakujące zdania) zajmują najwięcej czasu, więc rozłóż siły: przeczytaj tekst raz do końca, potem rozwiązuj luki. Krótkie zadania słownikowe rozwiązuj szybko – tu liczy się znajomość słów, nie czas namysłu.

flash.back: Zdanie nie jest pewne – nie możesz uznać go za udowodnione.
wyrażenia przeciwstawne – zapowiadają zmianę kierunku myśli
w rezultacie – po nim następuje skutek

flash.front: Ile trwa arkusz rejonowy i ile ma punktów?
Dwa zdania w zadaniu z brakującymi zdaniami są ...
flash.back: zbędne – nie pasują do żadnej luki.

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem (1–8) i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE). Za każdą poprawną odpowiedź otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
Buzzing above the traffic: why cities are becoming homes for bees

When most people imagine a beehive, they picture a quiet meadow or an orchard in the countryside. Yet over the last decade, hundreds of beehives have appeared in places that would have seemed absurd to our grandparents: the rooftops of hotels, office towers and even a famous opera house. Urban beekeeping, once a curious hobby, has grown into a movement that attracts both enthusiasts and serious researchers.

One reason for its popularity is a surprising discovery. Studies carried out in several European capitals suggest that city bees often produce more honey than those kept in farming areas. The explanation lies in the food supply. Modern agriculture relies on huge fields of a single crop, which flower for only a few weeks, leaving bees hungry for most of the year. A city, by contrast, offers a mixture of parks, gardens, balconies and street trees that bloom at different times from early spring until autumn.

However, the idea is not without critics. Some ecologists warn that keeping too many honeybees in one place can harm wild pollinators such as bumblebees and solitary bees, which compete for the same flowers. 'Honeybees are not endangered,' says biologist Elena Marsh. 'Many wild species are. Placing a hive on every roof may feel like helping nature, but it can actually make things worse.' She suggests that city authorities should focus on planting more flowers and leaving some grass uncut instead of promoting new hives.

Beekeepers answer that their work has other benefits. Hives on school roofs give pupils a chance to observe nature at close range, and some companies use the honey as a gift for clients, which improves their image. There are practical concerns, too. Beginners are usually required to complete a course, register their hives and keep them at a safe distance from busy pavements. Stings are rare, because bees that are well looked after are calm and prefer to fly upwards, high above the heads of passers-by.

Whatever one thinks about the debate, the story of urban bees shows how flexible nature can be. Cities, so often described as grey and lifeless, may turn out to be useful allies in protecting insects, provided that people plan carefully and listen to scientists as well as enthusiasts.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia; opisane badania i osoby są fikcyjne.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, z którego usunięto 7 zdań. Dla każdej luki wybierz literę (A–I) oznaczającą brakujące zdanie tak, aby otrzymać spójny i logiczny tekst. Uwaga: 2 zdania zostały podane dodatkowo i nie pasują do żadnej luki.
groups.text:
Most of us do everything possible to avoid being bored. We take out our phones in queues, put on headphones on the bus and switch on the television the moment we get home. (1)___ Psychologists, however, are beginning to suggest that this habit may be costing us more than we realise.

In one small experiment, volunteers were asked to sit alone in a quiet room for fifteen minutes, with no phone, no book and nothing else to do. (2)___ Many admitted afterwards that the time had felt much longer than it really was. Yet when the same people were later tested on creative tasks, those who had been bored for a while came up with more original ideas than those who had spent the same time on a simple, undemanding activity.

Researchers explain this result in the following way. (3)___ It starts to wander, connecting memories and facts that normally remain separate, and this is exactly how new ideas are born. Constant entertainment, on the other hand, keeps the mind busy with other people's content and leaves it no room for its own.

Children are an interesting case. (4)___ Teachers report that pupils who are given a few minutes of free time between tasks often return to work more focused. Parents, meanwhile, are often tempted to fill every free hour with lessons and activities, which can make it harder for a child to learn how to entertain themselves.

This does not mean that we should switch off all our devices for good. (5)___ The problem begins when we use them automatically, without noticing, simply to avoid an empty moment. A better approach is to choose some small times in the day, such as a walk to school or a journey by train, and to leave the phone in the pocket.

(6)___ After a few days, many people find that the discomfort disappears and is replaced by a feeling of calm. They also notice details around them that they had never seen before. (7)___ In a world that never stops offering something new to watch, learning to do nothing for a while may be one of the most valuable skills of all.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
bank: The first attempts may feel unpleasant, so it is worth being patient.
Silence and empty time have come to feel almost uncomfortable.
Boredom, it seems, is not an enemy to be defeated but a quiet teacher.
At first, the participants looked restless and kept checking their empty hands.
Some researchers disagree and claim that creativity cannot be measured at all.
Young children are usually quite good at inventing games out of nothing.
In a boring moment the mind is no longer given any task.
Phones and tablets are useful, and nobody needs to feel guilty about using them.
Boredom is also one of the most common reasons why teenagers give up their hobbies.

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE).
groups.text:
Typing is faster than writing by hand, and for most adults a keyboard is now the main tool of everyday communication. Yet a growing number of schools in several countries are bringing handwriting lessons back into the timetable, and researchers say they have good reasons.

One of the main arguments concerns memory. In a small study, students who took notes by hand during a lecture remembered more of the main ideas a week later than those who typed everything on laptops. The researchers believe that handwriting forces people to listen carefully and to summarise, whereas typists tend to copy sentences word for word without really thinking about them.

Another benefit may be connected with young children. Teachers report that pupils who learn to form letters with a pencil recognise them faster than those who only press keys. Writing also develops the small muscles of the hand, which are needed for many other everyday tasks, from buttoning a coat to using scissors.

Not everybody welcomes the change. Some parents argue that children will spend their adult lives typing, so valuable lesson time should be devoted to keyboard skills. There is also the problem of speed: pupils with untidy handwriting may feel discouraged when they cannot read their own notes, and teachers admit that marking handwritten work takes longer.

Most experts, however, do not recommend choosing one method over the other. A sensible compromise, they say, is to teach children to write by hand in the early years and to introduce typing gradually later, so that they can use both skills depending on the task.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, z którego usunięto 6 zdań. Dla każdej luki wybierz literę (A–H) oznaczającą brakujące zdanie. Uwaga: 2 zdania zostały podane dodatkowo i nie pasują do żadnej luki.
groups.text:
Almost everybody feels nervous before speaking in front of an audience. Some people get dry mouths, others shake or forget the first sentence. (1)___ Psychologists explain that this reaction is a leftover from the time when humans had to react quickly to danger.

When we feel threatened, the body prepares to run or fight. The heart beats faster, breathing becomes shallow and muscles tense. (2)___ A presentation, however, is not a dangerous animal, and the energy has nowhere to go.

Experts recommend several ways of dealing with this problem. The first is thorough preparation. (3)___ Speakers who have rehearsed their talk several times usually worry less about forgetting words.

Another useful technique is to slow down the breathing. (4)___ Taking a few deep breaths before going on the stage can calm the heart and make the voice more steady.

It also helps to change the way we think about stress. (5)___ Some studies suggest that people who tell themselves 'I am excited' perform better than those who repeat 'I am calm'.

Finally, it is worth remembering that the audience is usually on the speaker's side. (6)___ Most people are too busy thinking about their own opinions to notice small mistakes.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
bank: When we are afraid, we usually breathe quickly and not deeply enough.
Most listeners want the speaker to succeed and are not looking for errors.
Public speaking is taught in only a few schools around the world.
In a primitive situation, this physical response was extremely useful.
Some speakers prefer to read their texts aloud from a sheet of paper.
Knowing the material well gives a feeling of control.
This is why even very experienced speakers admit that they feel a little afraid.
Instead of trying to hide the excitement, we can treat it as useful energy.

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem (1–9) i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE). Za każdą poprawną odpowiedź otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
The town of Westbury lies beside a wide, slow river, and for most of its history the river was a danger rather than a pleasure. Every few years a child fell in, and in 2009 a tragic accident made the local council decide that something had to change. 'We could have built a fence along the whole river,' says councillor Ruth Palmer, 'but we chose to teach children to swim instead.'

The programme began with a single evening class at the town's old swimming pool, which was about to be closed because it needed expensive repairs. Parents paid a small fee, and a group of retired teachers and lifeguards offered to work as volunteers. Within a year, the pool was fully booked, and the council found money to renovate it.

Today every pupil in Westbury must complete a swimming course before the age of eleven. Lessons are given during school hours, and children who cannot afford swimming costumes can borrow them from the school. The course does not end with swimming skills: pupils also learn how to recognise dangerous currents, how to help a friend in trouble and when to call for help.

The results have been impressive. In the last six years there has not been a single accident on the river, and the pool has become a social centre where adults take part in water exercise classes in the evening. Neighbouring towns have started similar projects, although some of them have given up because they could not find enough volunteers.

Critics of the programme say that it takes time from other subjects and that a small town should not spend money on a pool when the roads need repairs. Ruth Palmer admits that the budget is tight. 'Nobody said it would be cheap,' she says, 'but I have never heard a parent say it was not worth it.'

(Tekst i dane zostały wymyślone na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, z którego usunięto pięć fragmentów. Dla każdej luki wybierz literę (A–G) oznaczającą brakujący fragment tak, aby otrzymać spójny i logiczny tekst. Uwaga: dwa fragmenty zostały podane dodatkowo i nie pasują do żadnej luki.
groups.text:
When the last cinema in the village of Marlow Bay closed in 2012, nobody expected that it would soon be the heart of the community again. (1)___ The building stood empty for two years, with broken windows and posters that had faded in the sun.

Then a young teacher, Daniel Webb, had an idea. (2)___ He gathered a group of volunteers and asked the owner whether they could use the hall for a single summer. The owner agreed, partly because he had no other plans for the place.

The volunteers started by cleaning and painting the walls. (3)___ Local carpenters repaired the old seats, and a nearby school lent a projector for the first screening.

The opening night was a big surprise. (4)___ People stood at the back and in the corridors, and the volunteers had to turn many neighbours away.

Today the cinema shows films four evenings a week. (5)___ Daniel says that this is exactly what he hoped for when he opened the doors for the first time.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
bank: Nobody was paid, but everybody was fed with sandwiches and tea provided by the café next door.
Daniel Webb teaches chemistry at the school and plays the guitar in a band.
On Sundays it becomes a place where grandparents and grandchildren meet to watch old classics together.
It soon became a sad sight for everyone who had grown up watching films there.
The village council plans to build a car park on the empty site.
He remembered how much he had loved the old cinema as a child and wanted others to share that feeling.
More than three hundred people came, although the hall had places for only two hundred.
